transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Simon Park (AE, Redwood), Riya Kapoor (SE, Redwood), Ayesha Khan (Nova - Platforms), Ethan Morales (Nova - ML Infra), Rohit Nair (Nova - Security)
Shared: Benchmark workbook (https://docs.google.com/sheets/d/novabench), slide deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/benchmarks-nova, repo: git.redwood/benchmarks/nova (link noted)

Summary: quick technical deep-dive to align on apples-to-apples benchmark protocol for runtime perf and on-prem vs hosted comparisons. Focus areas: prompt sets, sequence length distributions, load generation, KV/K V cache warmup, batching strategy, quantization artifacts, network/V P C constraints, and security artifacts needed for pilot.

Topics:
- Prompt set and user journey sampling
- Load generator configuration and traffic replay
- KV cache (prefix caching) behavior and warmup protocols
- Batching policies and impact on tail latency
- Quantization profiles and correctness checks
- VPC / on-prem networking and KMS integration
- Benchmark comparison normalization (apples-to-apples)

Action items (captured in metadata): see list

Transcript body:
[00:00] Simon: okay thanks everyone for joining, uh we're gonna run for about an hour, the goal is to lock down the benchmarking protocol so the on-prem pilot can run smoothly. Riya and I will mainly drive perf/ops questions.
[00:18] Ayesha: thanks, yeah we've got a set of internal SLAs and some real traffic traces, want to make sure the test mirrors production like for like. we also need to validate encryption and audit logs.
[00:32] Riya: perfect. quick question up front — are you looking at generator-style workloads (many short chats) or long-sequence single requests? we should pick a distribution because batching and KV cache behave very differently.
[00:48] Ethan: it's mixed; about 70% short prompts under 128 tokens, 20% mid-length 128-512, and 10% long >512. p95 for us is critical, p99 is a hard stop for some customers.
[01:05] Simon: right, so for apples-to-apples we'll need to lock sequence-length buckets and per-bucket QPS. we'll provide a starter prompt set that mirrors those ratios. also, note that our runtime's kernel selection and quantization can change perf per bucket.
[01:22] Rohit: on security, we need SOC2 artefacts, HSM/KMS diagrams, and confirmation on audit log retention. also the V P C peering path for on-prem is important.
[01:35] Simon: yes we'll share SOC 2 and the KMS flow. For on-prem—there are two modes: private control plane with customer-managed network, or fully air-gapped package; the pilot will use VPC peering and restricted egress.
[01:50] Ayesha: good. let's talk KV cache: we saw in earlier runs that warmup impacts first-minute tail latencies a lot. what's your recommended warmup protocol?
[02:03] Riya: we recommend a deterministic warmup: replay representative prefixes at low concurrency until cache hit-rate hits a threshold — e.g., >90% KV hits for the prompt set. we'll supply a warmup script. note: transcription here sometimes writes K V cache — in audio it was KV.
[02:22] Ethan: how long does that usually take per model? some of our larger models take longer to fill caches because of longer key widths.
[02:30] Riya: depends on model and sequence length distribution. operationally we capture a per-token cache hit curve; for medium models it might be ~5-10 minutes at low qps, for larger 8-16 minute. we'll include a warmup-time estimation table in the workbook.
[02:48] Simon: important to include the cache-warmup time in the experiment — some teams forget and compare cold-start latency to steady-state. apples-to-apples means you specify whether results are cold, warm, or steady-state and include the warmup procedure.
[03:05] Ayesha: agreed. next — load generation. we want to replay actual traces if possible. what tools do you recommend?
[03:12] Riya: we typically use a hybrid approach: replay trace for arrival pattern, but drive requests with our synthetic generator that can parametrize prompt lengths, user think-time, and concurrency. we'll share JMeter/Locust configs and a Kubernetes job for the generator.
[03:26] Ethan: will that generator also hit Dedicated pools or the private cluster? we need to ensure network path replicates production egress and ingress throttles.
[03:34] Simon: yep, for on-prem tests the generator should run in the same VPC/subnet as the infer nodes to capture intra-cluster networking. for hosted vs dedicated comparisons we run the generator from the same region to avoid cross-region variance.
[03:48] Rohit: a note on encryption — we need to validate KMS integration end-to-end; does your on-prem package support external HSMs?
[03:57] Riya: yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations; for the private package we document the kay management flows and can run a test encryption-only pass. we'll provide the diagrams and sample integration steps.
[04:10] Ayesha: quantization — we care about latency/cost wins but cannot accept quality regressions. what's your proposed stepwise quantization protocol?
[04:19] Riya: two-phase: first perf sweep across quant profiles (e.g., int8 symmetric, int8 per-channel, 4-bit mixed quant), capturing throughput and latency; second, quality checks using our eval prompt set and a small human review panel for hallucination/regression. we'll also provide delta metrics (EM, BLEU, or whatever is relevant).
[04:39] Ethan: do you have an automated regression harness? we want deterministic scoring for the pilot.
[04:44] Simon: Redwood Optimize includes quality-monitoring hooks that can run evals post-quantization and produce regression alerts. for the pilot we'll give you scripts to run locally and upload logs to the workbook. note: some of this was mis-transcribed in prior notes as 'Reedwood Optimize' — it's Redwood Optimize.
[05:00] Riya: also, make sure the eval set is the same across hosted/dedicated/on-prem runs; otherwise you can't compare. we will lock the eval prompt set in the sheet as a single source of truth.
[05:13] Ayesha: what about batching — we have strict latency SLOs; our users are sensitive to tail latency spikes when you batch too aggressively.
[05:21] Riya: batching policy should be expressed as two params: max batch size and max batching latency (e.g., 5ms/10ms/50ms). we recommend running experiments across that 2D grid and plotting p50/p95/p99. some kernels prefer smaller batches with multiple stream slots, others need larger to maximize throughput.
[05:38] Ethan: and continuous batching vs fixed-window?
[05:40] Riya: runtime supports continuous batching and fixed-window; continuous often yields better latency/throughput tradeoffs, but behavior changes with sequence-length mix. we'll capture both.
[05:49] Simon: make sure you specify tokenization and sequence padding rules — different tokenizers change effective seq lengths and batching density. include tokenizer version in metadata.
[05:58] Ayesha: yes, we'll attach tokenizer artifacts. on the comparison front — how do we normalize for hardware differences? our on-prem nodes are slightly older than your dedicated pools.
[06:08] Simon: for apples-to-apples we recommend: normalize by effective hardware FLOP or by normalizing to a reference model/runtime config. options: (1) run on identical instance types where possible; (2) if not, report per-token cost adjusted to base instance using a microbenchmark; (3) report absolute latency and relative cost. we'll put a normalization section in the workbook with formulas.
[06:28] Ethan: I like the microbenchmark idea. can you share a small kernel-level perf test?
[06:33] Riya: yes we'll share a microbench binary and scripts. note: kernels change with sequence length and quant profile, but the microbench gives a stable baseline for normalization.
[06:43] Rohit: network egress — if you run hosted vs private, we need to capture egress bandwidth and TLS termination differences. please document the TLS path.
[06:51] Simon: we'll document TLS termination and record bytes transferred per request in the workbook. also we recommend capturing client-to-inference hop latencies separately from inference time to separate network noise.
[07:03] Ayesha: about measurement cadence — should we run long-running steady-state runs or multiple short bursts?
[07:09] Riya: both. recommended protocol: 3 phases per experiment: cold-start (single request), ramp (10-15 minutes ramping to target QPS), steady-state (30-60 minutes at target). collect per-second metrics and compute p50/p95/p99 across last 80% of steady-state. document the seed for randomization in load generator.
[07:30] Simon: also capture GC/pagemap metrics on host and GPU memory utilization. we will supply host-side exporter configs.
[07:38] Ethan: for on-prem we have constrained GPU memory; quantization might let us fit bigger context windows — can that be included as a test axis?
[07:46] Riya: absolutely. include max_context as a variable and measure throughput vs context. quant profiles often reduce memory footprint allowing larger KV caches and bigger contexts.
[07:56] Ayesha: any gotchas for rolling canaries during the pilot?
[08:00] Simon: just one — if you do canary swap with a different quant profile, make sure the canary set uses identical prompt distribution; otherwise you will bias the canary. and include automatic fallback to the previous model if regen error rate or latency crosses threshold.
[08:15] Rohit: on audit logs, we need immutable audit trail for inference requests; does Redwood provide that for private?
[08:22] Riya: yes, we can enable request-level audit logs and ship them to your SIEM. retention policies are configurable. we'll include sample config.
[08:33] Ayesha: excellent. let's capture a concrete protocol in the workbook — column-based so we can run multiple experiments reproducibly.
[08:40] Simon: agreed. we'll provide the sheet with rows: experiment_id, model, quant_profile, batch_size, max_batch_latency_ms, context_window, tokenizer_version, warmup_procedure, warmup_duration_sec, seed, load_generator_config, hardware_profile, notes, and result links.
[09:00] Ethan: and can we add a column for 'expected business impact' so PMs can prioritize experiments?
[09:05] Simon: good call, we'll add that.
[09:09] Riya: quick note — sometimes transcripts write product names weirdly; earlier we saw 'Redwood Dedicate' — it's Redwood Dedicated. small but worth clarifying for shared docs.
[09:18] Ayesha: okay last thing: for on-prem pilot timeline — we want two-week pilot after configs are locked, and then scale to 8 weeks if results look good.
[09:26] Simon: timeline sounds reasonable. we'll aim to send the benchmark workbook and starter configs within 2 business days.
[09:34] Riya: i'll attach the KV-cache warmup script, locust/JMeter configs, and quant profiles to the repo.
[09:40] Ayesha: thanks, that's helpful.
[09:44] Simon: quick recap of next steps: 1) Redwood sends workbook + prompt/eval set + warmup script; 2) Nova shares representative traces and target SLAs; 3) sync to schedule pilot week (target first week of July); 4) Redwood shares SOC2/KMS diagrams and microbench artifacts.
[10:05] Ethan: noted. any blockers from security?
[10:08] Rohit: no blockers, just need the diagrams and a short threat model.
[10:13] Simon: we'll include a 1-pager threat model.
[10:16] Ayesha: thanks all.
[10:18] Simon: thanks, we'll follow up with the links and action items.
[10:22] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional mis-heard acronyms (V P C, K V). there is some crosstalk in places; timestamps are approximate.

Attachments referenced: benchmark workbook (link above), starter warmup script (git.redwood/benchmarks/nova/warmup.sh), microbench binary and scripts (git.redwood/benchmarks/nova/microbench), SOC2 + KMS diagram PDF (to be shared).

End of transcript.
